frameNumbering: One-based, row-major 4 columns by 3 rows in the rendered dark contact sheets
evidence: Direct visual inspection of all 18 contact/<group>/<example>.png rendered frame sheets. This is a sequential drawing audit, not a real-time playback measurement.
scope: Frames 5 through 12, their entering and exiting changes, and the 12-to-1 loop join. File validity, alpha reconstruction, and crop correctness were deliberately not used as proxies for animation quality.

overall.verdict: Not ready for a quality animation release
overall.rootCause: The repeated 1-to-6 generic blink consumes half of each 12-frame clip. Several unrelated key poses are then inserted at frames 7 to 10, followed by a sudden reset. At 15 fps this compresses blink, reaction, and return into 0.8 seconds, before the resting hold. Twelve existing drawings are not twelve coherent inbetweens.
overall.loopFinding: Most frame-12-to-frame-1 pairs approximately restore the same expression. The loop boundary is generally less serious than the discontinuities inside each clip. A good endpoint match does not validate the middle.
overall.repairRule: Give each clip one action. Remove the automatic leading blink unless blinking is the action. Use frames 1-2 as the stable starting state, 3-6 as progressive movement, 7-8 for the readable peak, and 9-12 for a gradual return. Keep the same eye construction and mouth stroke throughout. Do not create black pupils, detached eyebrows, or open-mouth cavities for only one or two frames without inbetweens.
overall.timingRule: Do not use a one-second endpoint hold to conceal a six-frame burst of unrelated poses. Timing holds may repeat a sound drawing, but every change of geometry still needs to follow the same action path. A longer one-shot is preferable to forcing two different actions into a nominal 12-drawing loop.

findings.issue: Both half-lidded eyes jump directly to full rings during reopening; the intervening mostly-open lid position is missing.
A substantial detached eyebrow appears above the right eye in one drawing, introducing a feature not present in the opening face.
The detached eyebrow vanishes in one drawing. This reads as a feature popping on and off, not an attentive lift.

clips.loop12to1: Near the same round-eye and closed-mouth pose; loop is not the principal defect.
clips.choreography: Keep a closed horizontal mouth and the same ring eyes. Make one soft attentive blink: lids descend progressively over frames 3-5, meet briefly at 6, reopen over 7-10, then settle at 11-12. Remove the detached eyebrow entirely from this clip. A listening eyebrow reaction can be a separate sequence.

findings.issue: Two skeptical half lids become two neutral rings at 6, then the left immediately becomes a heavy half lid again at 7. The one-frame neutral face is not an inbetween for the intended asymmetry.
The right open ring drops directly to the low skeptical lid; there is no intermediate height.

clips.loop12to1: Similar skeptical endpoint, with small drawing differences; internal eye-model changes dominate.
clips.choreography: Begin with both skeptical lids. Raise only the right lid progressively in 3-6 while keeping the left lid and mouth stationary. Hold the asymmetric doubt at 7-8, then lower the right lid in 9-12. No preliminary blink or simultaneous neutral-ring face.

findings.issue: The reopened eye construction changes from directional pupils inside a lid shape to centered ring eyes instead of preserving the up-right gaze through reopening.
A flat mouth becomes a completed smile in a single drawing, with no small curvature increment.
Both pupils jump back up-right while the smile becomes a straight bar simultaneously. This is a reset key pose, not a return inbetween.

clips.loop12to1: Close match to initial up-right glance and flat mouth.
clips.choreography: One recognition: keep the existing eye contour, bring the up-right pupils toward the user over 3-5, and lift the mouth corners gradually over 4-7. Hold at 7-8; return gaze and mouth gradually over 9-12. Do not spend the first half on a blink.

findings.issue: Frame 5 uses a flat horizontal eye cut with vertical-sided pupil openings, then jumps into the full worried eye contour at 6. This is a different construction rather than a near-open version of the same eye.
The straight mouth instantly turns into a full smile.
The completed smile instantly flattens again. The emotional gesture occupies three key poses without a build or release.

clips.loop12to1: Worried eyes and flat mouth approximately match; return inside the clip is the failure.
clips.choreography: Keep the soft inward-sloping eye silhouette. Ease both lids down only slightly while the mouth corners rise through four clear increments. Hold a small reassuring smile for two drawings, then reverse the increments. Avoid the unrelated rectangular half-eye at frame 5.

findings.issue: Mouth changes from a straight bar to a filled round dot to a wide outlined open grin in three consecutive drawings. These are three different mouth topologies without a continuous opening path.
Round eyes instantly become high closed arches at the same moment the mouth becomes a grin.
The residual grin and low lids disappear into neutral open eyes and a bar in one step.

clips.loop12to1: Near-neutral endpoints; no major endpoint-expression mismatch.
clips.choreography: Use one small smile that opens progressively: shallow curve, narrow open smile, medium open smile, peak. Raise the lower lids steadily into happy crescents alongside it. Hold 7-8 and return through the same family of mouth apertures. Remove the filled dot surprise mouth and the separate leading blink.

findings.issue: Both rightward-looking skeptical eyes jump to a left-looking asymmetry, while the mouth rotates sharply. There is no shared motion path between the two whole-face designs.
The left ring eye acquires a protruding lid/brow wedge, while the other eye changes outline and loses its open contour. These are feature-model changes rather than small motion increments.
Asymmetric eyes and tilted mouth snap back to the original pair of heavy lids and horizontal mouth.

clips.loop12to1: Similar initial and final heavy-lid face; the multi-feature reset occurs one frame earlier.
clips.choreography: Keep gaze fixed in one direction. Gradually raise the left lid while lowering the right lid a little and tilting the mouth by a small amount. Peak at 7-8, then reverse over 9-12. Maintain the same pupil and upper-lid construction at every height.

findings.issue: The eye rims add small lid nubs and develop a break against the pupil as the gaze moves up. The same ring construction is not maintained through the glance.
A completed smile appears in one drawing.
Gaze resets at 10, then smile resets at 11. This staggered sequence is made of endpoint swaps rather than gradual recovery.

clips.loop12to1: Near-matched neutral pose; internal new rim details and smile pops matter more.
clips.choreography: Use one upward recall glance. Keep the mouth horizontal. Move both pupils up-right over 3-6 inside unbroken eye contours, hold at 7-8, and return through 9-12. Recognition with a smile should be a separate clip if it needs its own acting beat.

findings.issue: The left eye drops immediately from a ring to a low half lid, while the right remains open.
Frame 8 alone replaces both eye outlines with open sideways crescent shapes. Frame 9 restores round eyes. This single-frame eye-model swap creates a visible flash.
The implied rightward glance resets through changing outlines and pupil placements rather than a consistent pair of eyes.

clips.loop12to1: Round-eye endpoint similar to initial pose.
clips.choreography: One deliberate rightward checking glance, with a slight left-lid narrowing. Keep eye rims closed and mouth fixed. Pupil displacement builds over 3-6, holds 7-8, and returns over 9-12. Never let the pupil remove a chunk from the outer silhouette.

findings.issue: Mouth runs bar, dot, smile, bar in four consecutive drawings. The discovery expression never develops along a readable mouth path.
Round eyes become large bell-shaped up-looking eyes in one frame, with entirely different bottoms and pupil positions.
The bell-shaped eyes abruptly return to the initial asymmetric eye model.

clips.loop12to1: Similar starting and ending asymmetric contours; the peak is disconnected from both.
clips.choreography: Keep the original eye models. Widen them moderately and enlarge a small mouth aperture through consistent oval shapes, then relax into the original closed mouth. If the intended discovery is pleased, choose a smile-opening action instead, but do not mix dot surprise, bell eyes, and smile in three frames.

findings.issue: Skeptical lids become asymmetric round eyes, then the left eye becomes a very tall vertical oval. This is a large silhouette leap rather than an overshoot supported by preceding drawings.
The tall eye instantly drops to a heavy lid while the surprised O mouth instantly becomes a frown.
Frown swaps to an upward smirk in one frame while the open eye drops to the original lid.

clips.loop12to1: Smirk and lid endpoints are close; does not rescue the disconnected center.
clips.choreography: Use a single surprised double-take without an intervening frown: lids lift in 3-5, both eyes widen with a small controlled overshoot at 6, recover slightly at 7-8, and lower through 9-12. Mouth moves from smirk to a small oval and back through narrow inbetweens. Keep both eye centers anchored.

findings.issue: Four consecutive whole-face designs: smirk, angry frown with open mouth, shouting grin, then happy wink. They have different eye contours, gaze, mouth direction, and aperture. They are key poses, not successive inbetweens.
The outlined mouth reverses from an upward arch to a large downward triangular cavity in a single frame.
Angry downward eyes become a ring-and-wink combination instantly. No recovery or hint of the playful turn precedes it.

clips.loop12to1: Approximate smirk endpoint match. The center is an unrelated facial montage.
clips.choreography: Choose one playful brow squeeze and a slightly widening smirk. Gradually angle the lids inward in 3-6, hold a restrained mock glare at 7-8, then relax in 9-12. Omit shouting and wink from this loop; they require separate one-shot clips with their own transition frames.

findings.issue: Low confident lids become inward-pointing open ovals then fully closed happy arches. The mouth likewise goes bar to curved smile to large open grin in two jumps.
The open-grin peak instantly collapses to the unrelated asymmetric smirk eye model, rather than returning through the same drawing family.
The remaining smile becomes a flat bar in one frame.

clips.choreography: Make one confident smile build: lift the mouth corners and gently squeeze the lower lids across 3-6, hold at 7-8, then relax over 9-12. Keep the smile closed for this restrained version. A broad cheering mouth can be a different clip.

findings.issue: Half-closed eyes jump to completely open circles; reopening could use one more mostly-open drawing.
Pupils jump directly to the far-right look. A quick saccade can be intentional, but the otherwise slow sequence has no anticipation and loses a useful middle position.
The two pupils return at noticeably different rates. The left stays near the right edge while the right moves leftward, briefly creating an inward convergence rather than a paired glance.

clips.loop12to1: Small pupil-position discrepancy, not a major silhouette failure.
clips.choreography: The existing eye construction is the most consistent in the set. Keep mouth fixed and omit the leading blink. Move both pupils the same normalized amount to the right over 3-5, hold 6-8, then return together over 9-12. This should be a focused repair, not a new eye style.

findings.issue: Both pupils jump from central to the upper eye edge, with no intermediate displacement.
Smile becomes a flat mouth immediately while the gaze holds.
Flat mouth becomes a completed smile immediately; it is a mood switch rather than a smooth waiting gesture.

clips.loop12to1: Matching smile and central-pupil endpoints apart from drawing drift.
clips.choreography: One patient upward glance with the same small smile throughout. Pupils ease upward in 3-6, hold 7-8, and return in 9-12. Keep the ring outlines, thickness, and mouth geometry fixed. A bored mouth change should be a separate acting choice.

findings.issue: The left full circle instantly becomes a deep half lid and the mouth immediately tilts, introducing the complete questioning pose at once.
Nearly held key pose uses visible changes of pupil location and mouth stroke angle without a clear directional action.
The left half lid jumps to a full ring while the mouth becomes level. The return has no intermediate lid height.

clips.loop12to1: The basic ring eye and flat-mouth pose matches reasonably.
clips.choreography: Start and end open-eyed. Lower the left lid progressively in 3-6 and tilt the mouth only slightly across the same interval. Hold 7-8 and reopen over 9-12. Keep right eye shape fixed and pupils looking at the same subject.

findings.issue: A separate curved lid above each dot vanishes, leaving featureless circular eyes. The drawing does not maintain a coherent single eyelid contour.
Black circular bites abruptly appear in both dot eyes to imply gaze. The face changes from pupil dots to white-of-eye discs without a transition.
Both black pupil notches vanish at once. This is a topology pop rather than a gaze return.

clips.loop12to1: Plain dot eyes and small smile approximately match.
clips.choreography: Keep eyes as solid dots. Communicate quiet company with one small coordinated eye-position shift toward the user and back, or a single coherent dot-to-line blink. Do not add black pupils inside an eye model that was originally the pupil itself. Mouth remains a small stable smile.

findings.issue: Plain dots acquire black notches at 7, then the left becomes a closed curved line while the right instantly returns to a plain dot at 8. Three eye models appear in three frames.
The flat mouth becomes a complete tilted smile with no curvature build.
Detached lid arcs appear above one eye, then both eyes, then disappear. These read as eyebrows flickering rather than a coherent wink reopening.

clips.loop12to1: Dot eyes and flat mouth match; the wink return before it is broken.
clips.choreography: One small one-corner smile plus a left wink. Keep the right dot fixed. Shape the left dot progressively into an oval, then a short curved lid, then reverse. Build and release the mouth corner over the same interval. Do not introduce black notches or detached brow arcs.

findings.issue: Small side-protruding caps on the dot eyes disappear at 6 then reappear at 7. The caps change eye construction without expressing a clear new action.
Four near-identical capped-dot poses provide no readable pride beat beyond small shape and position drift.
The caps vanish again in one step while the smile remains almost unchanged.

clips.choreography: Use one contented smile-and-squint. Solid dot eyes shrink vertically into small relaxed arches through coherent intermediate silhouettes while the smile deepens a little, then reopen along the reverse path. Avoid side caps and separate brow features. Keep eye spacing and the smile center fixed.

acceptanceBeforeReplacementRelease: Review every adjacent frame pair from 1 through 12 and the 12-to-1 join on the actual dark-background composite.
Watch the full clip at intended speed and at half speed; a contact sheet alone cannot validate temporal feel.
A visible feature may appear or disappear only through a continuous opening, closing, occlusion, or movement path, not because the generator chose a different face model.
The mouth stays in the chosen emotional family and follows a single opening or curvature path. No bar-to-dot-to-smile topology jumps.
Paired pupil motion preserves binocular direction unless deliberate convergence is the named action.
Each clip must still communicate its named action when played without the gallery title.
A new independent reviewer must reject visible middle-frame discontinuities even if asset count, layer reconstruction, and runtime unit tests pass.
